episodes.title: Concussive Trauma: A Hidden Layer in Trauma-Informed Practice
episodes.description:
Most concussive injuries are never clinically recognized. Underdiagnosis is particularly pronounced among women, survivors of intimate partner violence, and individuals whose injuries occurred outside athletic contexts. As a result, unrecognized concussive history is widespread in the trauma and chronic illness populations that clinicians routinely treat.

Post-concussive presentations are clinically complex. The same client may carry autonomic dysregulation, dissociative phenomena tied to loss of consciousness or medical exposure, and tissue-level injury with its own pathophysiology. These layers are rarely conceptualized together in trauma-informed practice and often result in partial treatment of a complex phenomenon.

This presentation by Dr. Maureen Keaveny draws on three somatic frameworks foundational to Dave Berger's Concussion and PTSD training: Somatic Experiencing's syndromal framework for chronic autonomic dysregulation, Ergos Institute's Eye of the Needle work with dissociative and altered states, and Dave Berger's Relational Bodywork and Somatic Education (BASE™), which addresses trauma at the level of body structures, organs, and tissues through attuned relational touch. Together, these frameworks illuminate a multilayered approach to post-concussive presentations and treatments.

episodes.title: Understanding Choice within the Context of a Cult
episodes.description:
Dr. Natalie Fabert from ASU and The Lalich Center on Cults and Coercion offers foundational knowledge and practical awareness to help clinicians provide competent care to self-identified cult survivors. 
 
Psychologically abusive, high-control groups, often called “cults,” exploit members through coercion and manipulation. Members may experience emotional, spiritual, sexual, or physical harm. While cults vary in form (religious, political, commercial, transformational), they tend to share key features: a rigid belief system, a charismatic and authoritarian leader, and a tightly controlled structure that discourages critical thinking and outside influence.

Survivors frequently struggle with moral injury, chronic shame, Complex PTSD, and other mental health concerns. Rebuilding life after leaving can be difficult, and many have trouble finding therapists who understand cult dynamics and recovery. Despite these needs, most clinicians receive little formal training on cultic abuse.
